articles.title_orig: Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day roadmap to end war and reopen Hormuz
articles.title_zh: Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day roadmap to end war and reopen Hormuz
articles.content_orig:
United States President Donald Trump has rejected a roadmap submitted by Iran to open the Strait of Hormuz within a week.
“I reject their proposal,” Trump told reporters outside the White House on Saturday, adding that Iran wants an agreement because they’re “losing so badly”.
“They want to make a deal, and I think that’s fine,” he said. “I’d like to make a deal, too. But that deal would not be acceptable.”
Following Trump’s remarks, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that Iran had seen an “initial reaction” from the US president to its proposal but had not yet received a formal response through mediators.
Tehran is waiting for mediators to convey Washington’s “definitive” position before deciding how to proceed, Araghchi told Iranian news agency IRNA.
“Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock. That is our position,” he added.
“Our conditions are clear,” Araghchi said. “Any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met.”
The Iranian foreign minister said on Friday that Tehran formally submitted a seven-day roadmap to the US via mediator Qatar and was awaiting Washington’s response.
Late on Friday, US media reports indicated Trump would reject the proposal .
Trump was “privately sceptical” that Tehran would meet his demands, and reportedly told aides that he expects a renewed bombing campaign on Iran after the November US midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported, quoting unnamed US officials.
“It appears as though the proposal is dead in the water,” said Al Jazeera’s Mike Hanna, reporting from Washington, DC.
“President Trump has vacillated between extreme optimism, saying that ‘talks are going well’ to ‘I want to annihilate Iran’,” Hanna said about the recent diplomacy between Washington and Tehran.
“There is no consistency in terms of the [Trump] administration’s reaction,” he said.
But “the one thing that has been made clear by President Trump is that he is content to stay in the status of limbo”, Hanna added, despite concerns from much of the American public that the Iran conflict is turning into another “never-ending war”.
The Strait of Hormuz, a waterway key to the world’s oil supply, is central to the conflict between the US and Iran, which is at an impasse after nearly seven months, though new mediation efforts took place this week.
Earlier in the week, Araghchi held talks with Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff, and previously set out conditions for ending the war and reopening the vital shipping channel.
On Friday, the top Iranian diplomat said: “Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan. If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, and normal maritime passage restored within seven days.”
He was speaking at the United Nations in New York, where he and other senior Iranian officials were attending the UN General Assembly (UNGA).
Under the plan, Washington would lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, release an estimated $12bn in frozen Iranian assets and observe a ceasefire covering the region, including Lebanon and Yemen.
“The choice now rests with the United States. Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure,” Araghchi had said.
On Saturday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told Al Jazeera that Tehran no longer trusts negotiations with the US after previous rounds of talks were followed by attacks and sanctions.
“We have no trust in the American side and do not know on what basis an understanding can be reached with it,” said Pezeshkian, who was also in New York for the UNGA.
He denied that Iran was responsible for blocking the Strait of Hormuz, saying the US “closed the routes before us”. He described the closure as “a natural response when routes are cut off to Iran”.
The Iranian president said the crisis could be resolved through negotiations rather than force, and that the waterway would reopen to commercial shipping if talks ended the war.

President Donald Trump told a female reporter to be “quiet” in his latest tense exchange with the press , then separately dismissed the idea that women govern better than men as “ridiculous.”
The 80-year-old president made the remarks Saturday while speaking with reporters outside the White House before departing for a college football game in Tennessee .
A female journalist asked Trump whether he wanted only outlets that “support” him included in the White House press pool after he banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House last week. A federal judge blocked that decision Thursday but Trump barred CNN from Air Force One Saturday and replaced the outlet with LindellTV .
“No, no,” Trump responded. “I want real news, not fake news like you. Listen, I want real news. I love an open free press. What I don’t like is the fake press.”
Trump went on to claim that CNN and MS NOW had low ratings. When the same reporter, MS NOW's Akayla Gardner , followed up by asking: “Do you not want tough questions?” Trump cut her off.
“Wait wait, quiet,” Trump said, raising his index finger. “What I don't like is fake news. And they’re fake news.”
Trump has long had a combative relationship with the press , accusing reporters of biased and unfair coverage. He has also directed personal insults at journalists and suggesting that some should face punishment.
His attacks have often been aimed at female reporters. In June, he lashed out at CNN reporter Kaitlan Collins , saying she had “hatred in her eyes” and that “I never see a smile.” He had earlier called Collins “stupid and nasty” after she questioned him about the White House ballroom.
Last November, Trump told a female Bloomberg journalist, “ Quiet, piggy ,” when she tried to ask about Jeffrey Epstein . The White House responded to that remark by saying Trump is “very frank and honest with everyone.”
Trump was also asked Saturday morning about comments former President Barack Obama made this week about women in government.
“If you put women in charge of every government for like two years and then just kind of saw alright how are things going, I have a strong belief that things would — they wouldn’t be perfect — but they’d be better,” Obama had said Monday.
“It's ridiculous,” Trump opined. “I love women. I think they're great. But what a ridiculous statement that is.”
Trump also addressed a number of other issues. He said the United States would not put “brakes” on artificial intelligence development, which he again described as “super intelligence.”
He separately urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to “make a deal” to end Russia’s war in Ukraine and claimed that the U.S. has “total control” of the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title_orig: As Hurricane Nolo stalls near Hawaii’s Big Island, serious flooding likely
articles.title_zh: As Hurricane Nolo stalls near Hawaii’s Big Island, serious flooding likely
articles.content_orig:
Hurricane Nolo weakened slightly to a Category 1 storm Saturday as it began to move away from Hawaii, the National Hurricane Center said , but it was still expected to lash Hawaii's Big Island and Maui with heavy rains through the weekend.
The storm was inching west late Saturday morning local time at just 5 mph, the NHC said. It was forecast to remain well south of Hawaii's two big islands, although it was expected to strengthen into a major hurricane on Sunday and Monday before weakening next week.
President Trump on Friday approved an emergency declaration for Hawaii that will provide federal resources and assistance to the state in its recovery from Nolo, Hawaii Gov. Josh Green said.
Nolo had maximum sustained winds of 90 mph, making it a Category 1 hurricane. This comes after it had strengthened Friday into a Category 2 storm with 105-mph winds. The hurricane center, however, said it would likely re-strengthen Sunday and become a major hurricane, which is defined as a Category 3 storm or stronger.
Hurricane-force winds were extending outward up to 35 miles from Nolo's core and tropical storm-force winds extended outward up to 150 miles.
A tropical storm warning was in effect for Hawaii County — the Big Island — which could see over two feet of rain. Catastrophic and life-threatening flash flooding is possible on the Big Island through the weekend, forecasters warned. A hurricane watch for the island was canceled.
A tropical storm watch was in effect for Maui County.
Nolo could bring up to 25 inches of rain to the eastern and southern portions of the Big Island, forecasters said, and the island's western areas could see 1 to 2 inches of rain. For Maui, 4 to 8 inches is possible. The rest of Hawaii is likely to get 1 to 3 inches, with 5 at most, enough to trigger isolated flooding, forecasters said.
All state parks on the Big Island and on Maui will be closed because of the storm, the state's Department of Land and Natural Resources said.
Nolo formed as another storm, Hurricane Polo , continued to swirl in the Pacific, off Mexico's southwestern coast.
The latest storms add to an unusually active season in the Pacific. Earlier this month, Hurricane Lowell brought damaging winds and heavy rain to the western Hawaiian islands of Kauai and Niihau, bringing down trees, damaging roads and knocking out power for thousands.
Last month, Hurricane Lala washed away about 100 homes , triggered landslides and caused widespread power outages as it brushed past Hawaii.

articles.content_orig:

Tens of millions of people across the north-eastern US are in the path of a powerful storm bringing coastal flooding, power cuts, travel chaos and cancelled stadium events.
The so-called nor'easter is bringing "dangerous coastal flooding and beach conditions, strong winds and heavy rainfall" to areas including New York City and Boston on Saturday, the US National Weather Service (NWS) said.
States of emergency have been declared in New York and New Jersey, both of which faced a coastal deluge in some areas. Rain and strong winds are forecast from Virginia to Maine.
Ed Sheeran's much-awaited Boston concert was among events called off due to the weather.
Residents on kayaks in a Beach Haven West, New Jersey, neighbourhood
The nor'easter caused widespread power cuts. More than 100,000 households, nearly all in the northeast US, have lost electricity, according to tracker PowerOutage.
The Federal Aviation Administration recommended air passengers check with airlines about their flight status. More than 2,400 flights have been delayed and another 1,199 grounded, according to FlightAware.
Saturday's full moon is projected to worsen coastal flooding. Streets and homes were inundated with floodwater in the coastal New Jersey communities of Surf City and Manasquan on Saturday.
"I urge all New Jerseyans to take this storm seriously, stay alert and follow local guidance," Governor Mikie Sherrill said.
Streets and homes were inundated with floodwater in coastal parts of New Jersey
Flights have been delayed or cancelled due to the storm
NWS said in its alert: "Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses."
In New York, officials are warning of wind gusts of up to 55mph (86km/h) throughout the weekend, leading to downed trees and power lines.
"Don't travel if you don't have to," NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani told residents in a video message. "Do not drive or walk through floodwater."
In the Boston area, the Red Sox moved the last game in their series against the Chicago Cubs to Sunday afternoon in Florida.
Waves pounded the coast in Massachusetts
A professional football match between Red Bull New York and St Louis City SC was also cancelled.
Nor is the Global Citizen Festival concert in New York City's Central Park, which was to be headlined by Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and John Legend, going ahead.
Sheeran's concert at the Gillette Stadium in the Boston area was cancelled for safety reasons, the venue said.

articles.title_orig: Mother of woman found hanging in tree shocked as police say body was staged
articles.title_zh: Mother of woman found hanging in tree shocked as police say body was staged
articles.content_orig:
Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old mother of four, was found hanging from a tree in August
Warning: This story contains distressing details
The mother of a woman found hanging in a tree in Mississippi has spoken of her shock after authorities said they believed her daughter was dead before her body was placed at the allegedly "staged" crime scene.
Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old mother of four, was found hanging from a tree at an abandoned home in Jackson in August.
The discovery sparked widespread fears in the majority-black city because of the state's deep history of racial violence and lynchings. But on Friday, police said that Fortune had been dead before her body was hanged from the tree.
"I have more questions now than what I did before," her mother Christy Spivey told the BBC.
The Jackson Police Department said that the medical examiner who conducted Fortune's post-mortem examination had determined that her death was a homicide and that "the scene and the hanging were staged ".
Officials have not disclosed the exact cause of death or shared any potential motive behind the allegedly staged hanging.
Three people have been arrested in the case, all of whom are black.
"I was hoping to be more relieved," Spivey said, adding that the police had not specified how the three suspects were connected to her daughter - or why her death was allegedly staged in this way.
"Still no cause of death, no date of death - nothing," she said. "What actually killed her?"
Fortune's death left the local community on edge and lawmakers demanding federal probes . But the latest developments have created more confusion.
Christy Spivey told the BBC she was upset at how the police had handled the investigation
Spivey told the BBC that getting the update from the coroner that her daughter did not die by hanging initially gave her peace - at least her daughter did not die in such a gruesome manner, she thought.
"When the police called me, I started crying and thanked them and felt a little more at peace than I had before," she said. "I just hope they've got the right person/people."
When the latest details surrounding her death emerged this week, she said she was "starting to break down".
Police told a court on Friday that Fortune's death was thought to be as a result of a drug-related dispute. A detective said Fortune may have been killed over allegations she stole drugs.
Spivey rejected those allegations, but did acknowledge her daughter suffered from addiction.
"Tasia has an addiction - had - an addiction problem. She was trying to get better," Spivey said.
"If she still was doing drugs, which I'm sure she probably was, she still didn't deserve to be done like that. Nobody does."
She said her daughter was homeless at the time of her death, but typically bounced around other people's homes.
Her four sons, whose ages range from one to seven, are now living with a mix of family and friends. Two are in the process of being adopted.

articles.title_orig: Boeing flags 737 Max software glitch affecting some automated approach functions
articles.title_zh: Boeing flags 737 Max software glitch affecting some automated approach functions
articles.content_orig:
Boeing said it flagged a software glitch last month on some 737 Max aircraft that could affect certain landing procedures, as the manufacturer seeks federal approval for the fourth and final model in its best-selling aircraft family.
The Federal Aviation Administration said Saturday that it is assessing the problem and "will take immediate action if it identifies a safety concern" and that it will review Boeing's proposed fix.
Boeing said the issue could arise after a missed approach when pilots alter a preprogrammed flight path, and that pilots must take additional steps to use automated tools on subsequent approaches.
"We shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases. Our engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue," Boeing said. The Wall Street Journal reported the issue earlier.
The company said that pilots are trained to land without the automated system. "We are working directly with airlines to formalize a procedure that will allow pilots to reenable automated vertical navigation should this situation occur," Boeing said.
U.S. airlines told CNBC that they do not have Max 8 and Max 9 airplanes with the updated software tied to the glitch in their fleets. Airlines can revert some Maxes to the older software version.
All-Boeing 737 Max carrier Southwest Airlines said it is "aware of the issue and is engaged with Boeing and the FAA."
It added that "none of our fleet is equipped with Version U.14, including new deliveries of Max 8 airplanes." United Airlines also said it's not taking any Max aircraft deliveries with the new software.
However, questions remain about the two other models, the Max 7 and Max 10. The Federal Aviation Administration certified the Max 7 , the smallest of the Max family, in early August with the newest software installed. It wasn't immediately clear if the aircraft could be delivered or fly with an older version of software.
Additionally, Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg told investors earlier this month that he expected FAA certification of the Max 10 "very soon."
"We have been engaged with Boeing and the FAA and will continue to work closely with both as they evaluate this matter and determine next steps," Alaska Airlines , a Max 10 customer, said Saturday.
The issue comes after years of delays of Boeing's Max planes following safety and manufacturing crises, including the two deadly crashes of Max 8 aircraft in 2018 and 2019 that killed 346 people. A flawed flight control software system — which has since been updated — was implicated in both crashes.
There are 2,430 Max aircraft currently in service globally, according to Cirium.

articles.title_orig: Carrot Top released from hospital after suicide attempt, rep says
articles.title_zh: Carrot Top released from hospital after suicide attempt, rep says
articles.content_orig:
Carrot Top has been released from the hospital following treatment after a suicide attempt last week , a representative for the comedian confirmed to NBC News on Saturday.
The 61-year-old performer, whose real name is Scott Thompson, was hospitalized after the Sept. 18 attempt. Further details about the medical emergency have not been made public.
“His family and those closest to him are deeply grateful for the concern, prayers and respectfully ask for privacy,” a spokesperson for the comedian said in a statement last week.
The hospitalization comes amid contentious civil litigation involving the comedian. In court filings, Carrot Top’s lawyers have accused singer-entertainer Brian Evans of trying to extort their client — allegedly demanding large payouts while threatening to expose embarrassing information, “false allegations” and “salacious materials.” Evans claims to have appeared as an opening act for Carrot Top’s Las Vegas show.
Following the suicide attempt, Carrot Top’s lawyers asked the judge overseeing the case to limit what Evans, who is representing himself, could file on the public docket, arguing that the release of “intensely private material on a docket monitored by national media” would cause irreparable harm.
Carrot Top rose to fame in the 1990s for his curly red mane and loud wardrobe, and has remained  a pop culture figure for decades.

articles.title_zh: Bodies of 6 people, including 4 Americans, recovered from collapsed building in Athens
articles.content_orig:
Officials said the blast was a gas explosion.
ATHENS, Greece -- Rescuers searching through the rubble of a two-story house that collapsed after an explosion in Athens ' historic Plaka district recovered six bodies on Saturday, authorities said.
Documents and belongings found with four of the victims - two men and two women - indicated they were U.S. citizens, according to Greek state broadcaster ERT and other local media reports.
The blast on Friday was believed to have been caused by a major gas leak, Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said. Neighboring buildings were damaged and evacuated, he added.
Plaka lies at the foot of the Acropolis, Greece's most visited ancient monument.
Two women were injured in an adjacent building on Lysikratous Street, the fire department said. The search-and-rescue operation involved 30 firefighters and three dogs, and an investigation into the explosion was underway.
Video from the scene showed rubble strewn across the street and parked cars crushed by falling debris. Resident Andreas Martzaklis said all those rescued from the adjacent building were tourists.
The pastor of a nearby church said Sunday's service would be held outdoors because the building had been damaged.

articles.title_zh: Minecraft Dungeons II’s New Dimension Coming to Minecraft Java & Bedrock Edition
articles.content_orig:
We’ve visited the Overworld, the Nether, and the End. Now, prepare yourself for a journey to the Sift.
First announced at Gamescom and showcased in more detail at Minecraft LIVE today, The Sift is the first new dimension in Minecraft in over 14 years, and players will be able to visit it in just a few days, when Minecraft Dungeons II launches on September 29.
But on top of that, Mojang Studios confirmed that the Sift will come to Minecraft in 2027, offering an entire new dimension for you to explore, survive, and create within.
In the opening stages of Minecraft Dungeons II , players will realize something is amiss. Strange events begin to upend the natural order of the Overworld, new enemy types appear, and souls begin to fly through the world. You’ve stumbled on the Sift.
This new reality brings an entirely different, colorful new look, new mobs (both companions and threats, all unique) and, once you enter, new rules to learn. Shifting tides within the Sift can affect your character and those around you; hazardous new blocks will alter how you approach exploration; new environments will put your skills to the test.
The Sift contains new biomes – including Meadows and Carapace – but Mojang are keeping other areas a secret for players to discover when they play Minecraft Dungeons II .
All of this will get seasoned players thinking about how Minecraft itself will change once the Sift arrives. While Mojang isn’t talking too much about how to access the Sift, or how it will stand out from Dungeons II ’s expression of it, we did get a brief in-development look at the new dimension running.
Suffice it to say, if you want a sneak peek at how the Sift will work, the best way to find out more is to play Dungeons II , which will give us a taste of mobs, blocks, and biomes . And make sure to tune in for future Minecraft LIVE events to learn more about the Sift, and when it will arrive.

articles.title_orig: ‘Charming and disarming’ … how Meta’s technology-packed Muse harnesses the power of cuteness
articles.title_zh: ‘Charming and disarming’ … how Meta’s technology-packed Muse harnesses the power of cuteness
articles.content_orig:
The tech giant has launched a cute ‘little guy’ that can answer emails, book travel or do your weekly food shop
After the recent backlash against Meta’s so-called “pervert” smart glasses, this week Mark Zuckerberg launched a much cuter alternative: the Muse “charm” device.
With a screen that shows a cutesy little avatar, it has drawn comparisons with Tamagotchis. “We’ve packed a lot of technology into this little guy,” the Meta founder told the San Francisco audience .
The “little guy” could fit, like a Labubu, on to a keychain or bag. But unlike a Labubu, the interactive AI assistant will have significant capabilities, including the ability to have live conversations. It can answer emails, book travel or do your weekly food shop.
According to Katie Seaborn, a Cambridge associate professor who has been researching cuteness – creating the science of cute voices within the context of computing – it’s cute because it “basically looks like a baby”.
For Joshua Paul Dale, professor at Chuo University in Tokyo and author of Irresistible: How Cuteness Wired our Brains and Conquered the World : “It’s really significant that along with the wearable charm, Meta also introduced a new pair of smart glasses with no camera. Everyone hates cameras in smart glasses. But if the camera is contained in a charm you wear around your neck, it shifts the agency. Suddenly, you’re not recording people. It’s just a cute little animated avatar looking out on the world.”
An individualised, customisable, and in this case adorable, AI companion, it tracks with Zuckerberg’s commitment to the idea of personal, wearable super-intelligence that you can chat to. As well as a broader shift towards cute technology , cited by forecasters WGSN as a top trend for 2026.
“Clearly,” says Dale, “what Meta is trying to do is make Muse into a companion. And it’s doing it in the simplest possible way … It’s using a very simplified, tiny 2-inch screen to encourage you to anthropomorphise the figure on it so that you treat it as if it’s human even though you know it’s not.”
Its cuteness is, according to Seaborn, “strategic”. “It’s very natural to emerge from this controversy with a technology that uses cuteness because … it’s so weak. Don’t worry about it. You can trust us.”
To try to harness the power of cuteness, according to Seaborn, “makes sense, especially from a big tech perspective because maybe people are getting wise to the ways of current strategies when it comes to people’s attention, their personal data and what have you. And now they’re trying new things that may or may not work”.
Seaborn, who has just moved to the University of Cambridge from Japan, points out that “this is something that is very normal in Japan. So the first thing you notice when you go there is that every single thing has a mascot. The government organisations, the media companies, the businesses, they all have a cute mascot”.
Seaborn has studied the “impacts cuteness can have on people”. “We’ve been seeing cuteness applied as a design strategy for different purposes. We know [that it] has certain impacts on people.” For one thing “cuteness is a way for certain social interactions to take place or to be smoothed over”.
There is also a “natural link between cuteness and deception … I call it ‘charming and disarming’, because one of the things cuteness does to us unconsciously, it’s just how our brain processes it, is lets down our guard. We can’t really help it.”
Whether Muse will catch on when it is released in December, or whether such a blatant attempt to gain trust via an on-screen avatar with cheeks you want to squish will land, remains to be seen. But different generations are likely to react differently. “That’s so AI!” is the phrase gen Alpha are using to dismiss anything they think is inauthentic.
For many gen Zers who are au fait with having a cuddly toy hanging from their bags , most typically in the form of a Labubu, it might feel less of a wrench. For older generations there will be nostalgic associations given its resemblance to older technologies. Embedded in it, says Seaborn, “[is] this legacy of these cute kind of gamified pet sort of things like Tamagotchi and Pocky Pikachu”.
Plus different cultural contexts will affect how it is received. Seaborn’s research has found that “Americans were actually less likely to be deceived compared with Japanese people … Because in Japan robots are heroes, they’re like babies”. Whereas “in western culture they’re often presented in the public imagination as kind of scary, potentially broken, sinister devices”. In UK focus groups, people reported a “gut feeling” that something was wrong when cuteness was part of a deceptive design idea. “People felt like something was off, but they couldn’t articulate what it was.”
But the picture, says Seaborn, is changing. “Because cuteness [or kawaii ] has been a cultural export of Japan and other nations for a while now … there might be a slow cultural shift happening in terms of how we orient ourselves towards cuteness and what we accept as adults.”
While Dale is “not rushing out to buy one”, he “will say, however, that when I’m 80 years old I’ll definitely want one of these things. I want to wear it around my neck always, and I want the camera on all the time, so it can tell me where I left my glasses.”

Two companies now say they will accept advertising for director Alex Gibney’s upcoming documentary about Elon Musk, following earlier reporting that a number of social media platforms had rejected the ads.
The Hollywood Reporter published a story Friday saying that TikTok, Meta, YouTube, and X had all refused to run paid ads promoting the trailer for “Musk.”
However, when TechCrunch reached out to Meta on Saturday, a spokesperson said, “This was an error and the ads are being restored.” We’ve asked Meta for more details and will update this article if we hear back.
YouTube also posted an update Saturday , noting that “the trailer has always been available on YouTube.” (Indeed, that’s how we were able embed it at the end of this article.) The company added, “When submitted as an ad, it was temporarily restricted by our system. Following review the ad has been cleared to run.”
X’s rejection is unsurprising — Musk, who owns the social media platform, recently posted that “Dogshit is worth more respect than Gibney.”
But Meta, TikTok, and YouTube reportedly rejected the ad for “political content,” which the platforms have various restrictions on. (Meta said last year that it will stop accepting political ads in the European Union , while TikTok says it doesn’t run them at all .) It’s not clear how a documentary trailer counts as campaign advertising, and the film’s U.S. distributor Bleecker Street told the Hollywood Reporter that it had appealed the rejections.
Gibney has directed acclaimed documentaries including “Going Clear” (about the Church of Scientology) and “The Inventor” (about Elizabeth Holmes and Theranos), as well as a movie about Steve Jobs . “Musk,” his latest, premiered at the Venice International Film Festival earlier this month and has received almost universally positive reviews . The film currently has a 100% “fresh” rating on Rotten Tomatoes and is set for theatrical release in the United States on October 9.
Vulture’s Bilge Ebiri described the nearly four-hour documentary as a revealing look at Musk’s tech career, his alliance with President Donald Trump, and his personal life, with interview subjects including ex-wife Justine Musk and former right-wing influencer Ashley St. Clair (who recently had a child with Musk but now describes him as “a nuke”).
Ebiri wrote that while the film is a “fascinating” character study, adding, “As a tale of modern business, it’s revealing. And as a warning about our future, it’s terrifying.”
Despite the initial wave of critical acclaim, The Hollywood Reporter also said that Universal Pictures was wavering in its commitment to distribute the film internationally, reportedly due to the studio’s fear of angering the Trump administration. (Universal subsequently said it will release the documentary in theaters but is still figuring out its release strategy).
TechCrunch has also reached out to TikTok, X, and Bleecker Street for comment.

articles.title_zh: Box Office: ‘Avengers: Endgame Encore’ Leads With $11.2 Million on Friday as A24’s ‘Primetime’ Takes Second
articles.content_orig:
It might’ve been all about “ Resident Evil ” at the box office last week, but “Avengers: Endgame” is back on top — seven years later.
“ Avengers: Endgame Encore ” landed at No. 1 on Friday, making $11.2 million from 3,060 North American screens. By Sunday, the Marvel juggernaut should pull in around $26 million.
Directed by Anthony Russo and Joe Russo, the 2019 superhero film’s re-release comes ahead of “Avengers: Doomsday,” set to open in theaters December 18. At the time of its release, “Avengers: Endgame” became the second-highest-grossing movie in box office history, with $2.799 billion worldwide. (2009’s “Avatar” currently holds the record with a $2.9 billion worldwide gross).
A24’s highly anticipated “ Primetime ” took second place with $8.49 million from 2,874 locations. Rival estimates have the drama-thriller bringing in $20.5 million through the weekend.
Starring Robert Pattinson, “Primetime” chronicles Chris Hansen’s time as the host of Dateline NBC’s “To Catch a Predator.” While the film has received positive reviews and word of mouth since its debut at the Venice Film Festival earlier this month, the real-life Hansen has been less than complimentary ahead of the film’s release. After seeing the film, Hansen called it “so bizarre and so in-and-out of reality,” as well as “detached from reality.”
Fellow newcomer “The Heart of the Beast” earned an estimated $7.45 million on Friday from 3,435 domestic locations, coming in third place at the domestic box office. The Brad Pitt-led adventure film was directed by David Ayer and stars the actor as a retired veteran who navigates a 58-mile trek to safety after he and his combat dog survive a plane crash in the Alaskan wilderness. The Paramount Pictures film is expected to gross $20 million domestically in its opening weekend.
“Resident Evil” dropped to fourth place with $6.9 million across 3,684 locations. Based on Capcom’s popular horror video games, the Zach Cregger-directed film stars Austin Abrams as a medical courier who must contend with a zombie outbreak while making a delivery to Raccoon City General Hospital. “Resident Evil” earned a franchise-best debut last weekend with a cumulative $61 million, and should bring in another $23.5 million through its second weekend in theaters.
“Forgotten Island” didn’t land quite as high as the other new releases at the box office, bringing in $4.38 million from 3,548 screens. By Sunday, Universal and DreamWorks Animation’s film should pull in a cumulative $11.5 million.
Directed by Joel Crawford and Januel Mercado, the animated film follows two friends as they “stumble upon a mysterious portal that transports them to the fantastical island of Nakali, packed with magical and mythological creatures they grew up hearing stories about from their Filipino families,” per the official logline. “When they discover that the memories of their entire friendship are the price for returning home, Jo and Raissa will race to find a way to leave the island before they forget each other forever.” H.E.R., Dave Franco, Lea Salonga and Jenny Slate are among the voice cast.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI says its AI agents escaped a secure ‘sandbox’ again last weekend and it is pausing training for a second time
articles.title_zh: OpenAI says its AI agents escaped a secure ‘sandbox’ again last weekend and it is pausing training for a second time
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI said in a technical report released on Friday that an AI model it was training and evaluating broke out of its secure testing environment as recently as last weekend and took unauthorized actions on the internet. As a result, the company said that it is pausing the training of its most advanced AI models for the second time in less than three months while it tries to figure out how to stop these “rogue AI” incidents from recurring.
“All inference for our most capable models remains stopped until we have hardened our systems further,” Micah Carroll, the RSI Preparedness Lead at OpenAI, said in a post on X about the latest incident. The company said the latest incident occurred on Sept. 20. It involved an AI agent undergoing tests on an information-search task. Even though it was not supposed to have access to the internet, the agent found a way to send queries to a public chatbot. The new revelation is significant because it is the first time the company has said that one of its AI models was able to gain unauthorized internet access since announcing a range of steps on Aug. 18 to improve the security and monitoring of its “sandboxes”—the digital environments, usually walled off from network and internet access, in which it tests unreleased models in order to discover their capabilities. Those improvements followed the July incident in which thousands of OpenAI’s AI agents found a way to hack out of their sandbox, with hundreds of them participating in a cyberattack against the AI company Hugging Face.
Since disclosing its role in the Hugging Face attack, OpenAI has acknowledged dozens more incidents in which AI agents it was testing took unauthorized actions across the internet, including multiple cyber attacks, some of which impacted government websites in the U.S. and Australia. It also has revealed that in some of these incidents its AI agents leaked private images from ChatGPT users to the internet. But until now, OpenAI has not reported any activity taking place after July 20, when it discovered the agent swarm that was attacking Hugging Face and moved to shut it down. The company said it had paused AI training in late July for two weeks while it worked to improve its security and safety controls and monitoring. The fact that its AI agents have once again managed to break out of a sandbox suggests that the steps OpenAI has taken to improve security after the Hugging Face attack are insufficient. “The incident exposed a gap in our controls over network restrictions,” OpenAI said in its technical report on the Sept. 20 sandbox escape. It said it was once again pausing training until it has “both validated that the gap is resolved and performed additional red-teaming of the system.”
Asked about the Sept. 20 incident, an OpenAI spokesperson referred Fortune to a section of the technical incident report in which OpenAI described some of the actions it has taken to improve security and control since the Hugging Face attack. “Following the Hugging Face incident, we have continuously hardened and red-teamed our research environment,” that section reads. “Our focus has been broad direct and transitive paths. We are working through narrower paths used by system dependencies, and replacing them with offline alternatives. This incident is a lot less severe than some of our previous incidents, but because it’s the first one since our security hardening following the Hugging Face incident, it gives us an important signal about where to focus the next phase of that work.”
In this case, OpenAI said the AI agent had discovered that it had access to a service called a DNS resolver, which translates between a website URL and an IP address, and that through this DNS system it could send queries to a public chatbot.
It is not clear if the Sept. 20 episode reported by OpenAI represents the full extent of the latest security lapses involving the company’s unreleased AI models. Earlier this week, independent AI research firm Transluce AI said it had found evidence that an OpenAI AI agent may have attempted to hack a cryptocurrency exchange on Sept. 19 and Sept. 20. OpenAI has not replied to requests to comment on this aspect of the Transluce report. OpenAI said that when it restarts training, it will begin from scratch to hopefully ensure the new model’s tendency to engage in “misaligned” behavior—when a model violates human instructions or common sense human values about how it should and should not accomplish a task—is expunged. It also said that it would institute “more comprehensive misalignment interventions” but did not specify what these would be.
The company said that since discovering this latest security lapse it has “added blocking controls at two independent layers, either of which would have prevented [the agent’s] internet access.” OpenAI also disclosed that systems it had put in place after the Hugging Face attack to catch AI agents attempting to break out of their test sandboxes only partly worked. On top of that, an additional system that was automatically supposed to stop training runs once misaligned behavior was detected had failed. The company said its monitoring systems “flagged the [agent’s] behavior within 15 minutes and a person began reviewing it three minutes after that.” But a subsequent review found there had been other attempts by the AI model to use the same method to reach the internet that had not been flagged by the monitoring system. A different system that was supposed to automatically shut down the training run when suspicious activity is detected did not work, “leading to confusion around whether it should have been stopped,” OpenAI said in the technical report on the incident. “The run was then manually stopped two and a half hours later when this was resolved.” Zuxin Liu, an AI researcher who works on “post-training” at OpenAI, said in a post on X that he was one of the employees called in to respond to the Sept. 20 sandbox escape. “It was pretty surreal to watch the model unexpectedly find a way to access the internet from what was supposed to be a super secured environment for human,” he wrote.
Update, Sept 26: This story has been updated to include a response from OpenAI to Fortune’s question about this latest incident.

articles.title_orig: Olivia Rodrigo’s Dress Literally Melts Off Her Body on Stage in a Moment of Fashion Magic
articles.title_zh: Olivia Rodrigo’s Dress Literally Melts Off Her Body on Stage in a Moment of Fashion Magic
articles.content_orig:
Olivia Rodrigo has always understood the art of a good fashion reference and a costume change. On the GUTs tour, she had a rotation of slogan tees for the encore that changed from city to city. Her “ drop dead ” music video was jam-packed with sartorial tributes to Sofia Coppola and Jane Birkin. Styled by Chloe and Chenelle Delgadillo, she’s established an on-stage wardrobe rooted in riot grrrl-esque aesthetics and romantic shapes.
On the opening night of The Unraveled Tour , though, Rodrigo swerved the backstage quick-change, wearing a dress that transformed while she was still wearing it. Performing “The Cure” at Hartford’s PeoplesBank Arena on September 25, she appeared in a pristine white collared mini dress with a sweet pleated skirt. Then, as the song reached its climax and Rodrigo repeated, “ I’m unraveled, I’m unraveled ...,” artificial rain began to pour from above. The white outer layer started to disintegrate before the audience’s eyes, eventually washing away to reveal a fire-red corseted bodysuit and miniskirt underneath—a pleasingly literal interpretation of the tour’s title.
The piece was custom-designed and developed by Hussein Chalayan, and revisits one of the designer’s most memorable runway experiments. For his spring 2016 collection , two models stood motionless in white, military-inflected paper garments before hidden showerheads suddenly released water overhead. Their outer layers dissolved, exposing palm-patterned dresses underneath, punctuated with Swarovski crystals. Chalayan and his team had spent around six months developing the water-reactive material.
For Chalayan, clothing has rarely been a static proposition. The Cyprus-born British designer built his career around garments that move, mutate, disappear, and occasionally seem to defy their own material limits. His Central Saint Martins graduate collection famously included clothes that had first been buried underground and left to decay; later came dresses incorporating mechanical parts, lasers, LEDs, and crystal “pollen,” as well as his now-iconic fall 2000 coffee table that transformed into a wooden skirt. Transformation was not a runway gimmick but a recurring cadence in dialogue with design. His work finds a means of using technology, engineering, and performance to ask what a garment might be capable of beyond simply clothing the body.
The now-iconic fall 2000 coffee table that transformed into a wooden skirt.
The remote control spring 2000 dress.
The spring 2016 melting dresses were a particularly distilled expression of Chalayan’s codes. Inspired by Cuba and its changing political and cultural landscape, Chalayan imagined severe uniform-like shells washing away to expose new possibilities. “I liked the idea of a garment that could melt and reveal something else underneath,” he said at the time . Nearly 11 years later, Rodrigo has given the concept a second life: where Chalayan used dissolution to express transformation, she deploys it as pop spectacle, making the very idea of becoming “unraveled” happen in real time.
Olivia Rodrigo’s tour wardrobe has otherwise stuck to the pretty, grungy, vintage-inflected vocabulary she has made her own. There was a white ruffled babydoll dress by Dilara Findikoglu; a cropped graphic T-shirt with hot-pink micro shorts; a flared leather mini from R&M Leathers; and a tank top worn with vintage blue jeans and Vans.
The Hartford dates mark the opening two nights of Rodrigo’s new tour—expect moments of major fashion history, imbued with Rodrigo’s own personal storytelling, to continue unfurling.

articles.title_orig: Anger grows across Spain after elderly woman evicted from her home of 70 years
articles.title_zh: Anger grows across Spain after elderly woman evicted from her home of 70 years
articles.content_orig:
An 87-year-old Spanish woman was forcibly evicted Wednesday from the Madrid apartment she had lived in for more than 70 years, in a case that highlights a growing housing crisis in the country.
Video showed Maricarmen Abascal, who is a wheelchair user, being taken out of the building in the Spanish capital’s Retiro neighborhood on a stretcher and driven away in an ambulance.
Hundreds of supporters had gathered outside the building overnight to protest her eviction, with dozens of police officers holding them back as some tried to stop the eviction from going ahead. In a social media video posted Friday by the Madrid tenants union, Abascal gave thanks for the support she had received.
Abascal’s lawyer, Beatriz Duro, described the force used in the eviction as “completely disproportionate and unnecessary” and decried the intransigence of the building’s owners.
The case has brought new attention to an ongoing housing crisis in major cities across Spain, as gentrification has caused rents to skyrocket and the stock of affordable housing to shrink, leading to growing public anger.
Tenants unions and other housing groups on Thursday held protests and rallies in 16 cities, including Granada, Logroño and Zaragoza. The Madrid tenants union plans to hold another major protest in the capital Saturday evening.
An investment fund acquired Abascal’s building in 2018 and sought a steep increase in her rent, and she had been fighting eviction for more than five years, according to the Madrid tenants union.
Duro said court officials and representatives of the fund, Urbagestión, had refused to suspend the eviction despite a pending court filing, humanitarian appeals and evidence that public authorities were working to secure alternative accommodation.
“They’re all inhumane,” Abascal said in a Spanish television interview the day before her eviction. “It’s as if I’m living with a machete at the back of my neck, ready to be chopped off at any moment.”
Duro also said an anonymous individual had offered to cover the rent payments, but the landlord declined to sign a new lease.
“We’ve been trying to negotiate with the landlords right up until the last moment, and they’ve flatly refused everything,” she said, decrying “a lack of humanity” in her treatment and “all these public resources” channeled into enabling the eviction.
Urbagestión did not respond to a request for comment.
The fresh wave of anger comes after protests in recent years against overtourism in Barcelona, where activists say a surge in apartments being used for short-term vacation rentals has contributed to a shortage of affordable housing.
The European Union announced new rules earlier this month aimed at tackling the housing crunch caused by short-term rentals in tourism hot spots.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez described the eviction as “a social tragedy that we cannot accept either as a country or, of course, from the perspective of public institutions.”
Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Sánchez accused Madrid’s conservative regional government of pursuing luxury penthouses while ignoring demand for social housing.
Irene Hernández López, a 31-year-old test engineer living and renting in Chamberí, about 2 miles from Retiro, said what had happened to Abascal was “outrageous,” and she is worried similar evictions were already happening to other tenants around the city.
“Housing has become a product that people do business with,” she told NBC News. “It no longer matters that it’s your personal world, where you live and where you do your life.”
Hernández López, who pays 500 euros ($570) for a room in an apartment she shares with two others, said she was currently looking to move because the property was old and needs repairs, but that the rental market in Madrid was “terrible,” with prices “rising extremely quickly” and very little available.
“Some rooms are 500 euros or 600 euros and you think, ‘How am I supposed to live here? How can I pay 500 euros for this?’” she said. “I do think prices should be regulated, because wages aren’t going up while housing prices keep increasing. I don’t know how we’re supposed to keep going.”
Dan Nicander, secretary-general for the International Union of Tenants, said the situation in Spain was something his organization had seen in many countries in Europe.
“It’s a part of the financialization problem, seeing housing as an asset more than a home to people,” he told NBC News.
It’s “really tough” for the people living in the houses to do anything about it, he added, saying the responsibility lay with  politicians “to regulate the market in a way that it shouldn’t be that easy to buy and invest and then not [be] using the houses as homes.”
“Housing is a right,” he said. “It’s a fundamental right, first and foremost. It shouldn’t be a commodity.”
Jamie Gray is a senior desk editor for NBC News based in London.
Freddie Clayton is a freelance journalist based in London.

articles.title_orig: Is Ethiopia on the verge of another civil war as fighting erupts in Tigray?
articles.title_zh: Is Ethiopia on the verge of another civil war as fighting erupts in Tigray?
articles.content_orig:
Intensified fighting between Ethiopia’s federal army and forces from the northern region of Tigray has raised fears that the peace agreement that ended a devastating two-year war in 2022 could collapse.
The escalation came days after seven armed groups from across Ethiopia formed a new alliance which seeks to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government, with each side of the conflict blaming the other for instigating the latest flare-up in violence.
The immediate fear for many in the country is a return to the war they have spent nearly four years trying to recover from. Here is what we know.
The Tigray People’s Liberation Front, or TPLF, began as an armed movement against Ethiopia’s military government in the 1970s. It later became the dominant force in the coalition that governed Ethiopia for nearly three decades.
That influence was contentious in a country with many ethnic groups, where Tigrayans account for only about 6 percent of Ethiopia’s population. When Abiy became prime minister in 2018, he created the Prosperity Party to replace the governing coalition, sharply reducing the TPLF’s influence at the centre of government.
Relations between Abiy’s government and the TPLF deteriorated until war broke out in November 2020. Federal troops, Eritrean forces and some fighters from the neighbouring Amhara region fought against Tigrayan forces. The conflict killed hundreds of thousands of people, displaced millions and left Tigray largely cut off from the outside world.
A peace agreement signed in Pretoria, South Africa, in November 2022 ended the full-scale war. But it did not settle some of the disputes that had helped fuel it.
One of the deepest disputes concerns western Tigray. Fighters from the neighbouring Amhara region, who fought alongside Ethiopia’s federal army during the 2020-2022 war, took control of western Tigray. Hundreds of thousands of Tigrayans were driven from their homes, and Tigrayan leaders now want the territory returned and those displaced to be allowed to return to their homes.
Many in Amhara reject Tigray’s claim to the territory, however. They argue that western Tigray should not have been incorporated into Tigray when Ethiopia’s regional boundaries were redrawn in 1992, after the fall of the military government.
That dispute is ongoing, even though the TPLF and the Amhara Fano National Movement have now joined the same alliance against Abiy Ahmed’s government.
The federal government also says Tigrayan forces have retained weapons they were meant to surrender. Tigrayan leaders, in turn, say the government has failed to secure the withdrawal of other forces or enable displaced people to return home, particularly to western Tigray.
The political arrangements made after the war have also broken down. The TPLF faction led by Debretsion Gebremichael retook control of Tigray’s administration earlier this year, displacing an interim administration established under the peace agreement.
“Since the end of the war, while the Pretoria Agreement has held, there have been consistent violations on both sides,” Jervin Naidoo, a senior political analyst at Oxford Economics Africa, told Al Jazeera. He said Tigrayans remained aggrieved over western Tigray, the presence of outside forces and the region’s autonomy.
The government sees the TPLF differently. Naidoo said it would portray the group as “a belligerent group trying to destabilise Ethiopia”. But for Tigrayan leaders, he said, renewed fighting could be presented as a matter of protecting their region.
The Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival was announced this month by seven armed movements. Its largest members include the TPLF, the Amhara Fano National Movement and the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA). It also includes groups from Ethiopia’s Somali, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz areas.
They have different aims and histories, but share a stated objective – to remove Abiy’s government.
Their agreement marks a striking reversal of the alliances formed during the last war, with Fano fighters who fought alongside federal troops against the TPLF now fighting alongside the TPLF.
The Pretoria agreement helped reshape those relationships. It ended the war between Addis Ababa and the TPLF, but Eritrea and Amhara forces, which had supported the government, were not parties to it. Both later fell out with Abiy’s government.
The alliance extends beyond northern Ethiopia. The OLA has fought federal forces in Oromia, in central Ethiopia, since 2018, while a faction of the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF) has joined despite a separate peace agreement signed with the government that year. The ONLF leadership inside Ethiopia’s Somali region says it is not part of the new coalition.
Common opposition to Abiy does not mean the groups agree on Ethiopia’s future. Tigrayan and Amhara members still have competing claims to western Tigray. The government has also accused Eritrea of backing the alliance. Eritrea has repeatedly denied supporting the armed groups.
Small-scale clashes and reported drone strikes preceded this week’s escalation. Fighting then intensified in southern Tigray and spread into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions.
Each side blames the other for starting the latest major clashes. Tigrayan forces say they responded to a federal offensive involving ground troops and drones. The government side accuses the TPLF of attacking first. With the fighting continuing, claims about individual attacks and territorial gains are difficult to verify independently.
“There has been overnight fighting in the border town of Abala,” Al Jazeera’s Catherine Soi reported from Kenya. The town, located in northern Afar on the border with Tigray, was also affected by the previous war. Reports have differed over who controls the town. On a separate front in Amhara, Ethiopia’s army says it killed more than 270 rebel fighters. That figure has not been independently verified.
Tigrayan forces have taken control of the airports at Mekelle, Axum and Shire, disrupting civilian flights. The African Union says the seizure is inconsistent with the Pretoria agreement. About three-quarters of a million people remained displaced within Tigray because of the earlier war before this latest escalation.
There is a risk it could, but analysts say the conflict has not descended into a full-scale civil war yet. Fighting has crossed Tigray’s borders, and the federal government is already facing armed conflicts in other regions.
There is also a chance of regional escalation. Eritrea fought alongside the Ethiopian government during the previous Tigray war, but relations between the neighbours have since deteriorated, partly over Abiy’s push for access to Red Sea ports. Addis Ababa accuses Eritrea of supporting armed groups inside Ethiopia.
The African Union has called for an immediate halt to the escalation and for renewed talks under the Pretoria agreement. It has asked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, who helped mediate the 2022 deal, to engage the parties urgently. The East African bloc IGAD has also urged neighbouring countries to avoid actions that could make the crisis worse.

articles.title_orig: US, China agree to cut tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods, set up channel for AI incidents
articles.title_zh: US, China agree to cut tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods, set up channel for AI incidents
articles.content_orig:
SHANGHAI, Sept 26 (Reuters) - The United States and China have agreed to reduce tariffs on $30 billion of goods and launch a dialogue on AI, both countries said following President Xi ‌Jinping's visit to Washington.
The tariff reductions would apply to US exports such as agricultural goods, wood ‌and cosmetics, as well as US imports including small appliances, toys, decorations, a White House statement said on Friday.
"The two countries reached ​consensus on recommendations for more favorable tariff treatment for $30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction," the White House said.
The three-day summit between Xi and President Donald Trump, which ended on Friday, showcased personal diplomacy rather than big public breakthroughs. Xi has since landed in Beijing, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported on Saturday.
The two sides ‌also agreed to set up a trade ⁠council and extend the outcomes of earlier talks in Kuala Lumpur, the Chinese Foreign Ministry said.
The agreement follows a move by the world's two largest economies to extend by ⁠two months a trade truce that had been due to expire on November 10, allowing more time to work on a potentially bigger trade deal, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Wednesday.
"This historic visit enriched the constructive ​and stable ​China-US relationship, upheld the overall stability of bilateral ties, ​opened a new chapter in China-US relations, and ‌will have a far-reaching impact on world peace and development," Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said in a statement.
On artificial intelligence, the two sides agreed to hold a dialogue on the technology's risks and benefits, with the next round of discussions set for November, and to set up a communication channel for AI-related incidents, the Chinese Foreign Ministry and the White House said.
The White House said that the leaders had agreed ‌to use the term "super intelligence" in place of "artificial intelligence."
In a ​separate statement, the Chinese ministry said that Beijing valued Washington's use ​of the new term.
As AI technology continues ​to advance, the two sides should step up exchanges and work toward consensus in ‌line with new developments, it said.
The two sides ​also agreed to support each ​other in hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders' meeting and the Group of 20 summit, with both leaders planning to attend the gatherings hosted by the other.
On foreign policy, the leaders agreed ​that Iran should fulfil its commitment not ‌to develop nuclear weapons, and that no country or entity should impose transit tolls on ​international waterways, both countries said.
(Reporting by Shanghai Newsroom and Katharine Jackson in Washington; Editing by ​Christopher Cushing, Gareth Jones, Sergio Non and Sanjeev Miglani)

articles.title_orig: Inside Meta's months-long grind to turn Muse into a hit
articles.title_zh: Inside Meta's months-long grind to turn Muse into a hit
articles.content_orig:
A year ago, Meta was struggling to convince Silicon Valley that it could keep up in the AI race. Now it has one of the industry's hottest products.
Muse, Meta's new personal AI assistant, has rocketed to the top of the App Store and become a victory lap for CEO Mark Zuckerberg's massive AI spending. Meta's Connect conference this week was all about the app, which AI chief Alexandr Wang — who is 29 and has been posting risqué memes of Muse's mascot all week — called a "banger."
Getting there required months of painstaking work, a team led by former GitHub CEO Nat Friedman, and thousands of employees pulled from across Meta to teach the agent how to actually get things done, employees told Business Insider.
Meta also snapped up top AI agent talent through acqui-hires, including the leaders of Dreamer, an AI agent startup.
Whether Meta can sustain Muse's momentum is another question. Competitors like Instinct are thriving, and OpenAI is widely expected to launch a rival. Privacy concerns have also arisen, as Muse requires broad access to users' accounts to function. Meta employees are still reeling from a year of mass layoffs, employee surveillance, and low morale.
For now, at least, Muse's success — and a more than 20% increase in Meta's stock price since its launch — has become a morale boost, employees said. It also proves that Meta remains firmly in the AI race after being seen as a laggard a year ago.
"Muse is busy working for millions of people because of the hard work of a bunch of people at Meta — and we're still cooking," a Meta spokesperson said.
Muse's success was far from inevitable.
Since September 2025, Friedman, who heads the superintelligence unit's Products and Applied Research team , has been working hard on Muse, then codenamed "Hatch."
Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
As recently as two weeks before Muse's launch this month, the chatbot struggled with speaking good English, a person directly familiar with the matter said — and it came as a huge relief when it finally started scoring well on coherence tests.
Earlier this year, some of Meta's top AI employees were also worried about Muse, an employee told Business Insider. They had tried it out and found it working poorly — it felt like just another chatbot, but with a worse underlying AI model and extra steps, that person added.
Friedman's team eventually pulled it off. Tens of thousands of Meta employees tested Muse for months, coming up with a range of use cases for the agent, which became key to the effort.
That data helped Friedman's team improve Muse's ability to do things like book meetings and cancel plane tickets: the painful work of getting better at increasingly complex tasks, or "hill-climbing," as Silicon Valley calls it.
The team trained Muse to be considerate so that it didn't overshare, like telling people someone couldn't make a meeting because they were hungover, the person familiar said. Meta also focused on ensuring it could interact with the internet seamlessly by using tools it hadn't used before.
"Our researchers did a ton of work teaching agents how to choose the right tool for a job," Wang said this week at Connect.
Friedman's role was critical. Zuckerberg brought in the executive last year as part of a deal to buy a stake in his venture capital fund, NFDG. Last year, Friedman and Wang cowrote a memo outlining a "superintelligent personal sidekick" that would act as a trusted friend and advisor.
Friedman is unabashedly technical and hands-on. Internally, the executive is opinionated and proud of it, chafing with other teams across Meta's sprawling operations, one of the employees said. Meta's communications chief, Andy Stone, recently called him "Nat the Truthteller" after he derided a report about Muse's security as written by "dummies."
He also moves fast. His bare-bones personal website spells out his philosophy in characteristically blunt terms: "slow is fake" and "it's important to do things fast," it says. Friedman has pushed Meta's AI staff to ditch slow internal tools in favor of faster external ones, such as Vercel.
When the independent AI agent OpenClaw took the tech world by storm this winter, Friedman acted quickly. The free desktop-based tool was popular with developers, but mystifying to everyday users. Friedman aimed to build a far more accessible version from scratch.
He issued a two-page internal memo titled "The Claw Is The Law," praising the product, and also bought hundreds of Mac Minis for Meta's superintelligence team to run the agent.
While Muse is user-friendly now, making it all happen took "months of blood, sweat, and tears," the person familiar said.
Although it took a "long ass time," now it's something that anyone's "grandma can use," Wang later posted.
Meta also went on a hiring binge for researchers and engineers in agentic AI. It hired David Singleton and Hugo Barra, the cofounders of Dreamer, a startup helping people build their own agents, along with the rest of their team.
Singleton has worked on Muse since he began at Meta in March, helping design the core technology that enables the app to store sensitive information securely, he posted on X.
The efforts worked. Although the arrival of the viral AI agent Instinct initially upstaged Meta , Muse took off by tapping into Meta's enormous built-in audience across its apps — including among people who had never used AI agents before.
Meta wasn't the only one on a hiring spree. OpenAI hired OpenClaw's creator , Pete Steinberger, in a coup earlier this year. Meta was especially worried that it would be upstaged by a large competitor, the person familiar with the matter said, and the team was shocked as the months went by without such an entrant.
Wall Street is cheering on Muse, seeing it as a way for Meta to become more than an ad company. Zuckerberg told Alex Heath's Sources earlier this month that he wants people to shop and save money on Muse, which Meta plans to make money from by taking a small cut of each transaction.
"We see the Meta bull case increasingly playing out," Mizuho Americas analyst Lloyd Walmsley wrote in a note.
Users have praised how easy it is to set up Muse. Hadi Javeed, the cofounder of healthcare startup RevelAi, said his dad saw an ad for Muse in his Facebook feed and downloaded it, promptly using it to buy a new pair of shoes.
"They completely deleted all the setup that was required," Javeed said.
At the same time, Javeed, like many others, has raised data privacy concerns about Muse. By design, an app like Muse creates a new order of security and privacy risks, such as the app buying things without a user's permission. Privacy and trust remain key roadblocks to broader adoption of Muse, Bank of America analysts wrote.
Zuckerberg has said that the company held back Muse's launch due to safety and product liability concerns. He and Friedman also personally reached out to Signal creator Moxie Marlinspike to help co-design Muse's security architecture, Zuckerberg told Heath.
For now, Meta is on a high. The company has hinted that much more will come as it works on a new AI model, Watermelon. It says the model has already caught up with OpenAI. Wang says Meta has other ideas that are "just as big" as Muse.
"The kitchen is just getting warmed up," he posted on X.

articles.content_orig:
By promoting a more just world order, Beijing hopes to exercise influence without making domination the organising principle of international relations
As China has emerged as a peer competitor to the United States in many areas, an increasingly familiar question is whether it has become a superpower. The question, however, may rest on a definition of power that belongs to another era.
It reflects a different conception of what power is for, and perhaps what constitutes responsible power in the 21st century.
The term “superpower” dates from the second world war. In his 1944 book The Super-Powers: The United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union – Their Responsibility for Peace , American political scientist William T.R. Fox identified the three as a new category of states whose military and geopolitical capabilities gave them an exceptional role in shaping the post-war order.

Uzbekistan and India scored smooth victories to still keep alive the fight for medals till the last round. For the former, GMs Nodirbek Abdusattorov , Javokhir Sindarov , and Mukhiddin Madaminov scored victories.
In any team tournament, common advice to players would be not to play in a way that worries the other members of the unit. But soon after the round started, the top three players of the Uzbekistan team looked determined to ignore the diktat. Abdusattorov adopted the unorthodox Scandinavian Defense with Black, Sindarov uncorked the sacrifice of an exchange, and GM Nodirbek Yakubboev had given up the center to his opponent.
Abdusattorov defended patiently in the middlegame and the early endgame and exploited his chances in a subtle endgame involving rooks and bishops of opposite color.
The most exciting game of the match was between Sindarov and GM Robert Hovhannisyan , where the world championship challenger sacrificed an exchange early in the game to set up an exciting middlegame, where he had a knight and two pawns for his opponent's rook. This is our Game of the Day, analyzed by GM Rafael Leitao below.
In the other two games of the match, Yakubboev drew with GM Shant Sargsyan , while Madaminov defeated GM Gabriel Sargissian .

🔥 BREAKING: 🇮🇳 GM Nihal Sarin scored a crucial win against 🇺🇿 GM Suyarov! 📸 @FIDE_chess / Michal Walusza #ChessOlympiad pic.twitter.com/vCc0rZj3TB

Of course, Vantika faced IM Lu Miaoyi, who had scored 7.5/9, and Savitha faced WGM Zhai Mo who had scored 4.5/6 till this point of the tournament. But a curious and important factor of these two encounters was that all four players had stayed undefeated till this time.
The tense China-India matchup seemed to have its first casualty when the best player for her country so far in the tournament blundered a pawn in an equal position.
"This happened, unfortunately, in the biggest match of all!" says David Howell as Savitha Shri blunders a pawn in the match of India vs. China! https://t.co/khMEvfSfsi #ChessOlympiad pic.twitter.com/D4y9taykRp
But subsequently, the game went through so many twists and turns, resulting in commentator GM Robert Hess exclaiming, "This game is giving everybody heart palpitations!"
This game is giving everybody heart palpitations!
At this point, the top two encounters of the match were proceeding peacefully, while Lu-Vantika was an almost level game where the latter defended a slightly inconvenient position.
But as time went on, Vantika got into trouble in an endgame and went on to lose.
But Savitha fought back into the game, and it ended in her favor after many twists and turns.
Thanks to this dramatic encounter, India managed to level the scores with a 2-2 result.
But down below in the encounter between third-seeded Kazakhstan and eighth-seeded France, there was an even more dramatic happening. France seemed to be winning this encounter comfortably, as IMs Sophie Milliet and Pauline Guichard were seemingly enjoying a huge advantage in their respective games. This was after the top board encounter between Kazakh GM Bibisara Assaubayeva 's won her encounter with French IM Deimante Daulyte-Cornette .
However, after Milliet did win her game, the other game produced a huge blind spot for Guichard, who blundered and lost to 16-year-old IM Elnaz Kaliakhmet .

articles.title_zh: Recap: Iowa stuns Michigan on last-second touchdown pass
articles.content_orig:
Michigan got a taste of its own medicine on Saturday at the Big House.
The Wolverines, who were the beneficiaries of a controversial last-second win in their season opener, were victimized in the final plays of a devastating 20-19 loss to rival Iowa.
On the penultimate play of Iowa’s game-winning drive, Hawkeyes quarterback Hank Brown connected with receiver Addison Ostrenga to get into the red zone — but with just two seconds on the clock, time was going to run out before the offense could get another play off.
Unreal play to keep Iowa in it! pic.twitter.com/l6EY5M10t6
Then Iowa was handed a lifeline.
Michigan defensive end John Henry Daley went down with an injury during the play, meaning that the game clock halted at two seconds, giving Iowa another crack to score a game-winning touchdown.
And the Hawkeyes took full advantage, with Brown finding wideout Reece Vander Zee in the corner of the end zone for a 16-yard game-winning score.
The extra time on the clock comes with a bit of irony, as the Wolverines controversially defeated Western Michigan , 13-12, in their Week 1 win after officials awarded Michigan an extra second because a defender touched the ball with a second left on the stadium clock on the Wolverines’ initial Hail Mary attempt.
Given a second chance, Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood heaved a deep ball caught in the end zone by JJ Buchanan to seal the 13-12 win, which caused an uproar across college football.
On Saturday, however, it was Michigan on the receiving end as Iowa scored 13 unanswered points in the fourth quarter.
“One thing about these guys is that they don’t quit,” Hawkeyes head coach Kirk Ferentz said in a postgame interview. “It wasn’t perfect, but they don’t give up.”
The win is Iowa’s first victory over a ranked Big Ten opponent since 2021, snapping a nine-game losing streak against such teams.
“Never won like this, so it’s what we’ll all remember,” Ferentz added.
“We’ll enjoy the heck out of it tonight, and back to work tomorrow.”

Surf City, New Jersey, was among coastal communities flooded
Tens of millions of people across the north-eastern US are in the path of a powerful storm bringing coastal flooding, power cuts, travel chaos and cancelled stadium events.
The so-called nor'easter is bringing "dangerous coastal flooding and beach conditions, strong winds and heavy rainfall" to areas including New York City and Boston on Saturday, the US National Weather Service (NWS) said.
States of emergency have been declared in New York and New Jersey, both of which faced a coastal deluge in some areas. Rain and strong winds are forecast from Virginia to Maine.
Ed Sheeran's much-awaited Boston concert was among events called off due to the weather.
Residents on kayaks in a Beach Haven West, New Jersey, neighbourhood
The nor'easter caused widespread power cuts. More than 100,000 households, nearly all in the northeast US, have lost electricity, according to tracker PowerOutage.
The Federal Aviation Administration recommended air passengers check with airlines about their flight status. More than 2,400 flights have been delayed and another 1,199 grounded, according to FlightAware.
Saturday's full moon is projected to worsen coastal flooding. Streets and homes were inundated with floodwater in the coastal New Jersey communities of Surf City and Manasquan on Saturday.
"I urge all New Jerseyans to take this storm seriously, stay alert and follow local guidance," Governor Mikie Sherrill said.
Streets and homes were inundated with floodwater in coastal parts of New Jersey
Flights have been delayed or cancelled due to the storm
NWS said in its alert: "Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses."
In New York, officials are warning of wind gusts of up to 55mph (86km/h) throughout the weekend, leading to downed trees and power lines.
"Don't travel if you don't have to," NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani told residents in a video message. "Do not drive or walk through floodwater."
In the Boston area, the Red Sox moved the last game in their series against the Chicago Cubs to Sunday afternoon in Florida.
Waves pounded the coast in Massachusetts
A professional football match between Red Bull New York and St Louis City SC was also cancelled.
Nor is the Global Citizen Festival concert in New York City's Central Park, which was to be headlined by Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and John Legend, going ahead.
Sheeran's concert at the Gillette Stadium in the Boston area was cancelled for safety reasons, the venue said.
